Two clans, the Han and Chu, vie to supplant the weak Qin ruler and forge China's first true dynasty. Historically, the Chu began in a stronger position, but the Han managed to defeat them. Chu Han is a trick-taking, climbing, and shedding game consisting of multiple hands. Players begin each hand with a mixture of Chu and Han cards, representing strains within clans, hostage taking, and shifting allegiances. Optional Events and two historical campaigns provide additional variety. Can you outmaneuver your rival to found a new dynasty? Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Chu Han 1.1 Game Objective 1.2 Game Setup 1.3 Gameplay 1.4 Key Categories & Symbols 1.5 End of Round & Scoring 1.6 Strategic Considerations Chu Han Chu Han is a tactical card game for 2 players (Han vs. Chu), simulating the historical conflict to claim the empire through card combinations and legendary characters. Game Objective Be the first to reach 31 or more Victory Points (VP) . Points are awarded at the end of each round based on remaining hand cards. Game Setup One player represents the Han (Blue), the other the Chu (Red). The deck consists of Troop cards (Values 1–9) in various colors and special Character cards. Each player starts with a hand of 15 cards. Gameplay The game is played over several tricks: 1. The player on lead , in either order: may play 1 LEAD power (click a card twice, turning it green, to play as a power), and/or may take a writ and draw 2 cards. 2. The lead player must play a set of 1+ cards, all the same rank. 3. The other player is then on response . They: may take a writ and draw 2 cards, and then must either play a higher rank set or pass. A set played on response must be the same number of card s as the set led (and of higher rank than the last set played). Continue step 3 until a player passes, yielding the lead. Then, discard all cards played. Key Categories & Symbols Troops (1-9): The foundation for all combinations. Characters: Unique cards with powerful effects that can shift the momentum. End of Round & Scoring A round ends when one player plays all their hand cards. The winner scores points both for cards remaining in their rival’s hand and for any writs that their rival took. If a player reaches the 31-point threshold , the game ends immediately. Strategic Considerations Timing: When is the best moment to play powerful characters to force the opponent to pass? Hand Management: Should I hold low cards for sequences or use them for quick tactical actions? [Rating: 1/10] A weird little game. I liked that it borrows the deck makeup from Great Dalmuti, but it takes out the player dynamics since it's only for 2. Risking giving more points to the opponent in exchange for drawing more cards is really neat, but the scoring is limited to 5 cards max, nothing dramatic. The events are pretty cool, but I hate having to read special powers on the 3s and 6s (this alone nearly killed it for me. and why are the special powers shown as SYMBOLS that make no sense? you're not using 90% of the card, just put text on it instead of trying to be MiNiMaLiSt).  There's a lot I like,

[Rating: 3/10] Absolutely broken balance with little counterplay from being trundled if RNG doesn't go your way. I'd at least prefer some chance to stabilize, even if your opponent has above average hands dealt to them in sequence.  It's just not very fun when your opponent is continuously dealt Ji Bu, and can just look at your hand the entire time. There is one counter in the game. Do not recommend. There are so many other fantastically balanced games of this type you can play - even with just a simple deck of playing cards.

[Rating: 4/10] Weird shedding game. You can get shut out and there seems to be no strategy. The cards have powers and you earned points.

[Rating: 4/10] The simple rules and limited choices make this game boring. The even deck helps a bit but not once during the 2 parties I played I felt im doing anything interesting or cool. The game looks nice and is space efficient but its pretty much all the positives.

[Rating: 4/10] Not sure I have played a game which was this long and this frustrating at the same time, while each hand goes quickly, it takes a really long time (over an hour easily) to get to 30. And that is when it was one-sided af. Of the 7 or 8 hands we played, I won exactly once. And that wasn't because I don't understand ladder climbing or trick taking. It was because of the hand of cards I got (kept getting) time and again, over and over. And there aren't enough (any meaningful) ways to mitigate a poor draw. [Rating: 5/10] Largely uninteresting shedding / climbing game with an arbitrary pasted theme that makes zero sense. Should have stayed abstract. Besides, it’s an unintuitive inversion of focus, where the tempo consideration of when you pass is more important that the rest of the game. There are some minor effects, but ridded with stupidity like „cancel your effect” and even „cancel your cancel” (in 2024 - it takes courage!).   Boring, mediocre, forgettable, uninspired. Doesn’t feel Tom Lehmann to me at all.

[Rating: 5/10] Not really sure if I like it or not. It is a solid climbing/shedding game, but the historical theme feels superficial at best. Definitely play with the Events. Otherwise, it’s pretty bland.

[Rating: 5/10] Seems fine for what it is. Not sure if it has anything at all to make me come back to it frequently, or at all. I'll give it some more plays, but definitely wish there was more 'umph' to this one.

[Rating: 5/10] A card shedding game themed with in ancient china. Players are trying to get rid of their hand by playing their cards and following based on the number of cards played or play a card for its action. While being the first player out yields the max of 5 pts (based on Cards), there are ways to score more points during the round based on cards actions. Unlike most card schedders, players can always opt for gaining more cards on Their turn, but if the opponent wins, they gain an extra point each time this is triggered.
